paraphrase: The world is false (mithyā) because it is seen, insentient and limited, like the silver seen in shell; falsity is defended under five definitions: not being the locus of either existence or non-existence (Pañcapādikā); being the counterpositive of the absence in all three times in the very locus of appearance (Vivaraṇa); being removable by knowledge (Vivaraṇa); being the counterpositive of an absolute absence in its own locus (Citsukha); being other than the real (Ānandabodha).
notes: Chapter 1. The five definitions and their ascription to earlier authors are recalled with moderate confidence; against Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta.

paraphrase: Ignorance is positive (bhāva-rūpa) and indescribable; it is established by the perception 'I am ignorant', by inference and by presumption, against the Dvaita objection that ignorance is only the absence of knowledge.
The mahāvākya conveys a partless meaning (akhaṇḍārtha): it does not predicate a relation between two things but indicates the one self through implication.
